title: 2014_PMC4256824_Determinants_of_vaccination_coverage_and_adherence_to_the_Greek_
ehr_evidence: parents and/or legal representative of the infant were asked to complete a brief questionnaire to obtain information on demographic and socioeconomic characteristics, health care providers and utilization of immunization health services. The infant was considered as immunized or not based on the immunization card, as provided by the National Greek Health Care System.
summary: A prospective convenience-sample survey of 1,667 infants aged 2-24 months in metropolitan Athens (2009-2011) assessing vaccination coverage and adherence to the Greek national immunization program and associated socioeconomic factors during the economic crisis.
key_findings: Overall, 1,667 infants were enrolled (mean age 13.1 ± 6.6 months, 51.5% boys); 4.9% (95% CI 3.9%-6.0%) admitted omitting a vaccine due to belief it was not necessary or potentially harmful.
Vaccination coverage was highest for DTP-IPV-Hib and lowest for hepatitis A (42.4%) and rotavirus (10.3%).
Use of the hexavalent vaccine was strongly associated with timely hepatitis B vaccination (97.5% versus 54.2% and 92.8% versus 25.7%, p < 0.01).
Minority children were less likely to receive the hexavalent vaccine (15.6% versus 32.4%, p < 0.01) but had comparable hepatitis B coverage (73.2% versus 80.9%, p = 0.16).

Multivariate analysis found parental age, occupational and educational statuses and family size (>3 children) independently associated with immunization coverage at 6 and 12 months (e.g., >3 children adjusted OR 0.36, 95% CI 0.21-0.63, p < 0.001 at 6 months; 0.42, 95% CI 0.24-0.72, p < 0.001 at 12 months).
Lack of insurance was not associated with missed vaccine doses (57.8%, 95% CI 55.1%-60.7%).
captured_features: vaccination coverage per vaccine (DTP-IPV-Hib, PCV, MCC, HepB, MMR, varicella, rotavirus, HAV)
pathologies_diseases: None as primary outcome; outcome is vaccination coverage/adherence to the Greek National Immunization Programme (vaccine-preventable diseases context).
population: 1,667 infants aged 2-24 months visiting a tertiary public outpatient clinic in metropolitan Athens, Greece, 2009-2011
exposure_domain: socioeconomic factors and economic crisis (parental age, education, occupation, family size, insurance, minority status)
limitations: Sample of convenience, not representative; overrepresentation of minority/urban working-class families and underrepresentation of higher SES and rural Greece.
Less stringent criteria used to define complete vaccination at 6 and 12 months, based on Greek pediatrician practices.
Potential sample bias from recruiting in an outpatient department.
